heard: NASA electriplated radioactive uranium onto a golden record heading into deep space. In 1977, the twin Voyager probes launched toward interstellar space carrying human messages. Led by astronomer Carl Sagan, the team packed 55 languages and whale songs onto disks. Each record was sealed inside an aluminum cover, featuring a map of 14 pulsars. If an alien civilization intercepts a probe, how will they calculate its age? This is why scientists placed a tiny, ultra-pure sample of uranium-238 on the cover. Because this isotope decays with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, it acts as a clock. Measuring remaining uranium and decay products reveals exactly when the spacecraft left Earth. No matter how long it drifts, this silent atomic clock tells the exact age. You
